missions.title: Password Fortress
missions.intro: Phantom is trying to guess the passwords to school accounts. He is counting on people choosing passwords that are too simple and leaving them where anyone can see. Make your defenses stronger!
facts: A strong password has at least 12 characters.
It mixes uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols: ! # _ & ? *
Don’t use your name, your birthday, your pet’s name or “123456”.
Use a different password for every site. Don’t write passwords on scraps of paper and don’t tell anyone, not even friends. Only your parents may know them.
Leaving the computer? Lock it (Win + L, or Control + Command + Q on a Mac) or log out of your account.
Two-factor authentication is a second lock: after your password, you also enter a code from your phone.

tasks.q: Password lab. Invent a made-up password that earns the “Fortress” level.
The computer lab. Emma went out for break and left her desk. Find 5 cyber-safety mistakes in the picture. Click on them right on the picture.

spots.name: Sticky note with a password
spots.why: Anyone walking past can read a password stuck on the monitor.

spots.name: Notebook “My passwords”
spots.why: Written-down passwords are easy to peek at or photograph.

spots.name: Unlocked account
spots.why: Emma left without logging out of the gradebook. Anyone can sign in as her.

spots.name: Someone else’s USB stick
spots.why: A USB stick you find can carry a virus. Never plug unknown USB sticks into a computer.

spots.name: Phone showing a code
spots.why: Everyone can see the text-message code. Lock your phone and don’t leave it unattended.

decoys.clock: The clock says break will be over soon. That’s not a threat!
decoys.cup: A cup of tea is no danger to security. Maybe to the keyboard!
decoys.keyboard: The keyboard has nothing to do with it. Keep looking!
decoys.mouse: The mouse is safe. Keep looking!

tasks.q: Which password is the strongest?

options.text: qwerty2013
Emma2014
Fluffy_Kitty!
Pizza#Moon&Fox7

tasks.explain: “Pizza#Moon&Fox7” is long (15 characters) and has uppercase and lowercase letters, a number and symbols. “qwerty2013” is just a row of keys, “Emma2014” is a name and a year, and a pet’s name is easy to guess.

tasks.q: Phantom made a list of passwords he will crack first. Which of these passwords are weak? Choose all that apply.

options.text: Alex2013
qwertyuiop
Zebra#Window!Tea42
password
Cloud_7_Cat&Oak

tasks.explain: “123456789”, “qwertyuiop” and “password” are on lists of the most popular passwords in the world, and they are cracked in a second. “Alex2013” is a name and a birth year. Long passwords made of different kinds of characters are much stronger.

tasks.q: Your best friend asks for your game password so they can beat a hard level for you. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them the password. They’re my best friend!
Type the password in the chat so they don’t forget it
Politely say no: only I and my parents know my password
Tell them only half of the password

tasks.explain: A password is like the key to your home: you don’t give it out, not even to friends. Friends can fall out, and a chat message can end up in the wrong hands.

tasks.q: You typed the right password, but the site also asks for a code that was sent to your phone. What is this called?

options.text: Two-factor authentication
A computer virus
Phishing
A website error

tasks.explain: It is a second lock on your account’s door. Even if Phantom learns your password, he can’t get in without the code from your phone. That is why you should never tell anyone a code from a text message.

missions.title: Don’t Take the Bait
missions.intro: Phantom sends out trap emails and messages and builds fake websites. He wants you to hand over your password yourself. This trick is called phishing, from “fishing”: the scammer throws out bait and waits for you to bite.
facts: Scammers pretend to be popular games, services, banks and even your friends.
Signs of phishing: rushing and threats (“your account will be deleted in 2 hours!”) and amazing gifts (“you won a smartphone!”).
Check the website address: the real game address is cubeworld.example. Fakes: cubew0rld.example (a zero instead of an “o”) or cubeworld.example.free-gift.example (it ends in someone else’s domain).
A green padlock and https at the start of the address mean the connection is secure. But scammers can have a padlock too, so the address itself is what matters most.
Real services never ask you to send your password or a code from a text message.
Spotted a trap? Don’t click anything, don’t reply, and show the message to an adult.

tasks.q: Sort the agent’s mail. Which messages are safe and which are phishing?

items.text: Your account will be deleted in 24 hours! Confirm your password at picloop-help.example/login
items.explain: Phishing: threats, rushing, a strange address and a request to type your password.

items.text: Congratulations! You won a new smartphone! Just pay $2.99 for delivery: short.example/prize-now
items.explain: Phishing: an amazing gift from a stranger and a request to pay.

items.text: Reminder: the field trip is tomorrow. We meet at 8:30 in front of the school.
items.explain: Safe: you know the sender, and there are no links or requests for passwords.

items.text: Hi! Vote for me in the contest: enter your phone number and the code from the text message here: vote-contest.example
items.explain: Phishing: your friend’s account may have been hacked. Never give anyone a code from a text message.

items.text: Please buy some bread on your way home.
items.explain: Safe: an ordinary request with no links and no passwords.

tasks.q: Someone sent you three links to log in to the game CubeWorld. The real game site is cubeworld.example. Which of these sites is the real one? Look carefully at the address bar.
tasks.explain: The real one is option A. Option B has a zero instead of the letter “o” and no secure connection. Option C only starts with cubeworld.example, but it is really the site free-gift.example: look at what the address ends with before the first slash “/”.

tasks.q: Your mom got a text: “Your bank card has been blocked! Urgently tell our operator the code you will get in the next text, at +1 202 555 0111.” What do you advise her?

options.text: Read out the code quickly before the card is blocked
Tell no one the code and call the bank at the number printed on the card itself
Forward the text to everyone she knows to warn them
Reply to the text and ask for an explanation

tasks.explain: A real bank never asks you to read out a code from a text message. The only way to check is to call the official number printed on the card.

tasks.q: Investigate the email. Find 5 signs of phishing by clicking on the suspicious parts. Be careful: every wrong click costs a point.

parts.clue: A fake address: a zero instead of the letter “o” and someone else’s domain. The real game site is cubeworld.example.

parts.text: URGENT!!! Your account will be deleted
parts.clue: Rushing and threats: scammers want you to act without thinking.

body.text: We noticed that someone logged in to your account from another city.
Within 2 hours, send us your username, your password and the code from the text message.
body.clue: Real services never ask you to send a password or a code from a text message.
The link leads to a fake site, not to cubeworld.example.

body.text: And as a thank-you for confirming, you will get 5000 crystals as a gift!
body.clue: An amazing gift is the bait on the hook.

missions.title: Secret Data
missions.intro: Phantom collects information about students from open pages and photos on social media. The less he finds, the safer everyone is.
facts: Personal data is information that can be used to recognize or find you.
Keep these secret: your home address, phone number, passwords, bank card details and photos of documents.
Photos can give away secrets too: a sign with your address, the school name on your uniform, a car number plate, a location tag.
Don’t tell people online when nobody is home, and don’t show everyone where you are right now.
You can share your hobbies: favorite books, games and drawings, without your address or private details.

tasks.q: Sorting. What can you share online, and what must stay secret?

items.text: My favorite cartoon
items.explain: This is a safe hobby. Nobody can find you with it.

items.text: My home address
items.explain: Strangers can use an address to find you.

items.text: My drawing of a cat for a contest
items.explain: You can share your creative work if the drawing has no personal data.

items.text: My phone number
items.explain: You give your phone number only to people you know in real life.

items.text: The password for my email
items.explain: A password is always a secret.

items.text: My favorite color
items.explain: This can’t hurt anyone.

items.text: A photo of my mom’s bank card
items.explain: Scammers can steal money with card details.

items.text: “We’re all going to the seaside for two weeks, the house will be empty”
items.explain: That is how burglars find out nobody is home.

items.text: The title of my favorite book
items.explain: Sharing favorite books is safe.

items.text: A photo of my birth certificate
items.explain: Documents contain a lot of personal data.

tasks.q: Emma wants to publish this post. Find 5 details that give away her personal information. Click right on the picture.

spots.name: Sign with the address
spots.why: With the street name and house number, strangers can find where Emma lives.

spots.name: School badge on the uniform
spots.why: The school name shows where Emma can be found every day.

spots.name: Car number plate
spots.why: A number plate tells things about a family. It is better to blur plates.

spots.name: Location tag “now”
spots.why: The tag shows exactly where Emma is right now. It is better to turn location off in posts.

spots.name: Caption about an empty house
spots.why: Never write that you are home alone and your parents are away: bad people can use that.

decoys.menu: Three dots are just the post menu.
decoys.sun: The sun shines on everyone the same. Keep looking!
decoys.window: An ordinary window. You can’t see anything.
decoys.tree: A tree won’t tell anyone where you live.
decoys.cat: The cat is lovely and harmless :)
decoys.smile: A smile is great! Keep looking.
decoys.likes: Likes are not a threat. The danger is somewhere else!

tasks.q: A message from a “game admin” says you won a prize and you must send your home address for delivery. What do you do?

options.text: Send the address. It’s a prize!
Send only the street name
Send nothing and tell my parents
Ask them to send the prize to my school and give the school’s name

tasks.explain: Real admins never ask for your address in private messages. It is a way to trick you into giving away your data. Show such messages to an adult.

missions.title: Digital Footprint
missions.intro: Everything you post online leaves a trail, like footprints in the snow. Phantom knows how to follow a trail. Learn not to leave too much behind.
facts: The internet remembers everything: even a deleted post may have been saved or screenshotted by someone.
Before posting, ask yourself: “Would I be okay with my teacher and my grandma seeing this?”
Make your profile private so that only friends you know in real life can see your posts.
Turn off location in posts and don’t show everyone your phone number or school name.
A stranger online may not be who they say they are. Don’t send them photos and don’t agree to meet.

tasks.q: Set up the privacy of Emma’s profile on the social network PicLoop. Flip the settings and see what a stranger can see.
tasks.safeMsg: A stranger sees only a name and an avatar. The profile is protected!
tasks.okText: Now Phantom can’t find out anything extra about Emma.

sets.label: Private profile
sets.why: An open profile can be seen by everyone, including strangers.

sets.label: Show phone number
sets.why: You give your phone number only to people you know, in person.

sets.label: Location in posts
sets.sub: Add a place to every photo
sets.why: Location shows where you go and where you live.

sets.label: Messages from strangers
sets.sub: Any user can write to you
sets.why: Strangers should not be able to write to you.

sets.label: Show school and class
sets.why: With the school name, it is easy to find you.

sets.label: Review photo tags
sets.sub: I can be tagged only with my permission
sets.why: Without a review, anyone can tag you in any photo.

tasks.q: You deleted an embarrassing post 5 minutes after publishing it. Is it gone forever?

options.text: Yes, deleted things disappear completely
No, someone may have saved it or taken a screenshot
Yes, if nobody liked it

tasks.explain: In 5 minutes, someone could have seen the post, saved it or photographed the screen. It is better to think before you post than to delete afterwards.

tasks.q: Think before you post. Which of these can you post online, and which can’t you?

items.text: A photo of my drawing from the art show
items.explain: OK: it is your own creative work with no personal data.

items.text: A video of my little sister crying, with the caption “haha”
items.explain: Not OK: it is humiliating, and your sister didn’t agree to it.

items.text: A screenshot of a chat with a friend, without asking her
items.explain: Not OK: you don’t post other people’s messages without their permission.

items.text: A photo of a concert ticket with the barcode showing
items.explain: Not OK: scammers can use a barcode to get in instead of you.

items.text: A review of a book I read
items.explain: OK: it is useful and safe.

items.text: A group photo from the field trip that all my classmates agreed to post
items.explain: OK: everyone in the photo agreed.

tasks.q: In a game, someone called “Max, 12 years old” writes to you. He wants to be friends, asks for your photo and suggests meeting in the park. What do you do?

options.text: Send a photo. He’s my age!
Agree to meet, but bring a friend
Don’t send a photo, don’t go, and tell an adult
Give him my phone number to get to know him better

tasks.explain: Anyone could be hiding behind “Max”, even an adult with bad intentions. Tell your parents or a teacher about such messages and block the user.

missions.title: Cyber Friendship
missions.intro: Phantom stirs up fights in chats because it is easier to destroy friendship and trust that way. A CyberShield agent knows how to stop cyberbullying and how to support others.
facts: Cyberbullying is bullying online: hurtful messages, mocking, sharing someone’s photos without permission, fake profiles, leaving someone out of a group on purpose.
If you are being bullied: don’t answer rudely, take screenshots, block the bully and report them in the app.
Always tell an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher or a school counselor.
Many countries have a free helpline for children. In many European countries it is 116 111. Ask an adult for the number in your country. Calls are free.
Don’t be a silent bystander: support the person being bullied and never forward hurtful things.

tasks.q: The class chat. Read the messages and choose what to reply. Your words decide how this story ends.
tasks.title: Class 6B chat

outro.text: You stopped the bullying, supported Ben and gave him the right advice.

script.text: Look how Ben fell over in PE 😂
Let’s make a meme out of it and send it to all the school chats!

script.ask: What do you write in the class chat?

options.text: Haha, yes! I’ll think of a caption
options.note: That will only make the bullying worse: the meme will spread around school and Ben will feel even worse. Try something else.

options.text: Don’t. Ben will feel awful. Jack, please delete it

reply.text: Actually, I wouldn’t like it either. Jack, delete it.

options.text: Write nothing, but quietly forward the photo to a friend
options.note: By forwarding the photo you take part in the bullying too, even if you say nothing in the chat. Try something else.

script.text: Was everyone laughing at me? I feel awful… I don’t want to go to school tomorrow.

options.text: Don’t worry about it. It’s your own fault for falling
options.note: Words like that hurt even more. Ben needs support right now.

options.text: I’m on your side. Let’s tell our teacher together. She will help

reply.text: Thank you… Okay, let’s do it together.

options.text: I didn’t laugh, so it has nothing to do with me
options.note: A witness to bullying can help too. Supporting a friend is very important.

script.text: Some anonymous account keeps sending me nasty messages. What should I do?

script.ask: What advice do you give Ben?

options.text: Reply with something even worse!
options.note: A rude reply only fuels the conflict, and the bully gets what he wanted.

options.text: Delete all your accounts and never go online again
options.note: Ben has done nothing wrong and shouldn’t have to hide. There are better ways to protect yourself.

options.text: Take screenshots, block the account, report it and tell your parents

reply.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for being there for me!

tasks.q: Which of these is cyberbullying? Choose all the correct options.

options.text: Writing hurtful comments under someone’s photo
Making a fake profile with someone else’s name and photo
Wishing a classmate a happy birthday in the chat
Leaving someone out of the class group on purpose and laughing about it
Sharing a funny cat video with a friend

tasks.explain: Cyberbullying is when someone is deliberately hurt, humiliated or shut out. Birthday wishes and funny cat videos don’t harm anyone.

tasks.q: You are being bullied online. Put the steps in the right order. Move them with the arrows.
items: Take screenshots of the hurtful messages
Block the bully and report them
tasks.explain: First, don’t add fuel to the fire. Then save the evidence, block the bully, and be sure to tell an adult.

tasks.q: Many countries have a free helpline for children. Which of these numbers is the child helpline number used in many European countries?
tasks.explain: 116 111 is a free child helpline in many European countries: you can call it if you are bullied or scared. Ask an adult for the number in your own country (for example, in the UK it is Childline, 0800 1111). 911, 999 and 112 are emergency numbers for police, ambulance and fire.

missions.title: Virus Attack
missions.intro: Phantom’s last strike: he planted infected files in the school network. Neutralize them before the malicious programs spread to the computers!
facts: Malicious programs (viruses, trojans) can steal passwords, damage files and spy on you.
They most often hide in “free” games, cheats, game currency generators and pirated software.
Be careful with files from strangers. A file called “photo.jpg.exe” is a program, not a photo: look at the last extension.
Never plug a USB stick you found into a computer.
Antivirus software and timely system updates are your shield. Is the computer acting strangely? Tell an adult.

tasks.q: File check. Which of these are safe to open, and which could be infected?

items.text: homework.docx
items.explain: Safe: a file from your teacher in the school service, and you were expecting it.

items.text: free_robux_generator.exe
items.explain: Dangerous: generators of free game currency don’t exist. It is a malicious program.

items.text: beach_photo.jpg.exe
items.explain: Dangerous: the last extension is .exe. It is a program that only pretends to be a photo.

items.text: Minecraft_FREE_crack.zip
items.explain: Dangerous: pirated “cracks” often contain viruses.

items.text: Security update for your system
items.explain: Safe: official updates close the “holes” that viruses crawl through.

items.text: USB stick “Class_photos”
items.explain: Dangerous: a stranger’s USB stick can infect the computer as soon as you plug it in.

items.from: Classmate · school email (you agreed on it)
items.text: science_project.pptx
items.explain: Safe: you know the sender and were expecting this file.

tasks.q: How can you tell that a computer is infected? Choose all the signs.

options.text: The computer suddenly became very slow
Ads and windows open by themselves
Friends get messages from you that you didn’t write
A new episode of your favorite cartoon came out
The antivirus suddenly turned itself off
The laptop ran out of battery after 5 hours

tasks.explain: Slowing down, strange windows, messages sent in your name and a switched-off antivirus are warning signs. Tell an adult about them. A battery that runs out after 5 hours is normal.

tasks.q: Final agent training. Flip the cards and find the pairs: a term and its meaning. The fewer moves, the more points.

pairs.meaning: A trick to get your password or money
A program that looks for malicious files
A code from your phone after the password
Information that can be used to find you

missions.title: Fake Detector
missions.intro: Phantom has changed his tactics: now he spreads made-up news to scare students and cause panic. A CyberShield agent can tell truth from fake.
facts: A fake is a false or twisted piece of news that is spread on purpose.
Signs of a fake: a screaming headline in capital letters, “SHOCKING!”, “Share this NOW!”, and strong emotions such as fear, anger or excitement.
There is no real source: “scientists proved”, “a doctor I know said”, “they are hiding the truth from us”.
Check the news on 2–3 reliable sites: official websites and well-known news outlets. If only one anonymous channel reports it, it is doubtful.
Photos and videos can be fake too: old ones, ones from a different event, or ones created by artificial intelligence.
Not sure it’s true? Don’t share it!

tasks.q: The news feed. Which messages look true, and which look fake? Pay attention to the source.

items.text: Repairs to the library on School Street begin on Monday. The reading room will work in the community center.
items.explain: Looks true: an official source, a calm tone and specific facts.

items.text: SHOCK!!! Smartphones make children grow a third eye! Share before they delete this!
items.explain: Fake: a screaming headline, an unbelievable claim and a demand to share quickly.

items.text: Tomorrow all schools in the country close for a month. A principal I know told me!
items.explain: Fake: an anonymous source and “a principal I know” instead of an official announcement.

items.text: Tomorrow: snow and temperatures dropping to -5 °C (23 °F).
items.explain: Looks true: an official weather service and an ordinary forecast.

items.text: Scientists proved it: if you eat chocolate instead of breakfast, your grades will go up!
items.explain: Fake: “scientists proved” with no names, a strange website, and news that is too good to be true.

items.text: On Thursday there will be a charity fair. All the money will go to help an animal shelter.
items.explain: Looks true: a familiar official source and a specific event.

tasks.q: Examine the fake post. Find 5 signs of a fake in it. Every wrong click costs a point.

parts.clue: An unknown, anonymous channel with a screaming name is an unreliable source.

body.clue: A screaming headline in capital letters and the word “SHOCK” are an attempt to scare you.

body.text: A doctor I know told me that smartphones make children grow a third eye.
body.clue: There is no real source, only “a doctor I know”.

body.text: Official websites say nothing about this because they are hiding it from us!
body.clue: “They are hiding it from us” is how the author explains why nobody else is writing about it.

body.text: SHARE WITH EVERYONE NOW BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!
body.clue: A demand to share right away, so you don’t have time to check.

tasks.q: Someone forwarded you suspicious news. Put the checking steps in the right order. Move them with the arrows.
items: Stop and don’t share it right away
Look at who the author is and what the source is
Search for the news on 2–3 reliable sites
If nothing confirms it, don’t share it and tell an adult
tasks.explain: First stop, then check the source, then look for confirmation in reliable outlets. No confirmation? Don’t share it.

tasks.q: A photo went viral on social media: a whale swimming in a school swimming pool. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: It’s true. A photo doesn’t lie
The photo could be edited or made by artificial intelligence, so it needs checking
If the photo has lots of likes, it must be true
I should forward it to my friends quickly

tasks.explain: Images are easy to edit or to generate with artificial intelligence. A lot of likes doesn’t make a photo true.

missions.title: Smart Phone
missions.intro: The final mission. Phantom wants to sneak into your smartphone through “free” games, open Wi-Fi and unnecessary app permissions. Protect your phone!
facts: Install apps only from official stores (Google Play, App Store) and with your parents’ permission.
Check permissions: a puzzle game doesn’t need your contacts, microphone, location or text messages.
Free Wi-Fi in a café or a mall can be unsafe: don’t type passwords or bank card details there.
“Free skins” or “pay $1 for 1000 coins” on other sites is a trap to steal your account.
Update your system and apps: updates close “holes” in your protection.
If your account is hacked, don’t panic: there is a clear plan of action.

tasks.q: You are installing the game “Kitty Puzzles”, and it asks for a lot of permissions. Leave on only the ones the game really needs.
tasks.safeMsg: The game got only what it really needs. Great!
tasks.okText: The game can save your progress, but it knows nothing about you or your friends.

sets.label: Saving progress
sets.sub: Keep completed levels on the phone
sets.show: The game can’t save your levels
sets.why: The game really needs this permission to remember your levels. You can leave it on.

sets.label: Access to contacts
sets.sub: Names and numbers of everyone in your phone
sets.show: Names and numbers of all your friends

sets.label: Microphone
sets.why: A puzzle game doesn’t need to listen to you.

sets.label: Location
sets.why: Puzzles don’t care where you are.

sets.label: Reading text messages
sets.show: Your text messages, including verification codes
sets.why: Login codes for your accounts arrive in text messages. A game must not read them.

tasks.q: You are in a café with open Wi-Fi called “FREE_WiFi” and no password. What should you definitely NOT do on this network?

options.text: Check the weather forecast
Log in to your parents’ online bank and type in card details
Read news on a well-known website
Listen to music

tasks.explain: On an open network, scammers can intercept data. Passwords, card details and banking are only for home or mobile data.

tasks.q: In a game, someone writes: “Free skins! Log in with your account at free-skins-game.example”. What do you do?

options.text: Log in. The skins are free!
Don’t click the link: it’s a way to steal accounts. Tell an adult
Give my password to a friend so he can check the site
Type only my username first, and the password later

tasks.explain: There are no free skins on other sites. It is phishing: logging in through such a site hands your account to scammers.

tasks.q: Disaster: your game account was hacked! Put the actions in the right order. Move them with the arrows.
items: Tell your parents or a teacher
Change the password from another, safe device
Warn your friends not to open messages sent in your name
tasks.explain: First, adults: they will help. Then a new password from a safe device, two-factor protection and a warning to your friends.

tasks.q: The final challenge! Find 6 cyber-safety words in the grid. Click the first and the last letter of a word. Words run horizontally (left to right) or vertically (top to bottom).
